Uranium. A heavy, silvery-white, weakly radioactive actinide metal and the heaviest naturally occurring element in significant abundance on Earth. All uranium isotopes are radioactive and decay over time due to atomic instability. It serves as the critical fuel source for nuclear power plants and is the primary fissile material used in the first nuclear weapons because of its uranium-two hundred thirty-five isotope.

Martin Heinrich Klaproth discovered uranium in seventeen eighty-nine in the mineral pitchblende and named the element after the recently discovered planet Uranus. In eighteen ninety-six, Henri Becquerel revealed the phenomenon of radioactivity when he discovered that uranium crystals emitted invisible rays capable of exposing photographic plates. Uranium is mined primarily as uraninite or pitchblende and refined into a concentrated oxide powder called yellowcake, composed mainly of triuranium octoxide. To separate isotopes, uranium is converted to uranium hexafluoride, a volatile compound fed into gas centrifuges or gaseous diffusion barriers to enrich the fissile uranium-two hundred thirty-five content. When struck by thermal neutrons, uranium undergoes induced nuclear fission, a chain reaction releasing immense energy that powers nuclear reactors. Alpha decay of uranium in the Earth's crust is the source of terrestrial helium gas. Uranium mineralizations frequently occur alongside gold in ancient conglomerates, allowing joint mining operations. In breeder reactors, neutron capture by uranium-two hundred thirty-eight produces uranium-two hundred thirty-nine, which decays into neptunium-two hundred thirty-nine and then into plutonium-two hundred thirty-nine.
